name: wiggle
desc: Program for applying patches with conflicting changes
why: Patch application that tolerates conflicting context is clever diff-matching work, though it is still a fairly niche utility.

brief.what_it_is: Wiggle is a command-line C program that applies patches whose context no longer matches the target file exactly, the cases where GNU patch would reject a hunk. It can also do word-wise diffs and three-way merges. Its inputs are one, two, or three files (use - for stdin), which can be patch files, merge output, or whole files. Output is the patched or merged text, with unresolvable conflicts marked, or a diff-style report. The help text describes four functions: merge (the default), diff, extract, and browse.
brief.why_it_exists: The author describes it as a tool to 'apply patches that patch rejects', and the repository's own description is 'apply rejected patches and perform word-wise diffs'. The problem is a patch whose surrounding lines have drifted, so a line-based tool gives up on the hunk.
brief.how_it_works: The README I could read is mostly the top-of-file comment and help text, which does not describe the algorithm. The help text says merge compares three files word by word and reports unresolvable conflicts as whole-line differences. The --lines option switches to line-wise comparison. The source has files named bestmatch.c, merge2.c, and patch_depends.c, which suggest a best-match search over candidate positions, but I did not read them, so treat that as a guess.

brief.install_notes: Nothing beyond the brew install was in the pages I read. The repository has an INSTALL file and a Makefile, so building from source is the expected route. I did not open INSTALL.
brief.standout: Most patch tools match whole lines. Wiggle matches word by word, so it can apply a hunk whose context has changed slightly and still produce a three-way merge with word-level conflict markers. It also has a diff mode that shows word-level changes.
brief.status: Maintained, though slowly. The latest tarball on the author's site is wiggle-1.3.tar.gz, dated 2024-02-01. The repository shows 329 commits and 111 stars. The source header says version 1.3, dated 2020-10-03. I did not find a last-commit date on the page.
brief.caveats: Licensed GPL-2.0 (the source header says GPL-2+). It is a niche utility. The browse mode's help text says it 'will eventually allow limited editing', so editing is not finished. The brew description calls it a fairly niche tool. I did not check platform support or build requirements.

entry.title: wiggle
entry.tldr: Wiggle applies patches that GNU patch rejects, matching word by word instead of line by line so drifted context still lands.
entry.deeper_look:
Wiggle is a small C program for the moment when `patch` gives up. A hunk's surrounding lines have changed since the patch was made, so a line-based tool cannot find where it belongs and writes it to a reject file. Wiggle compares at the level of words, which lets it place many of those hunks anyway. Where it cannot, it marks the conflict in the output.

It does four things: merge (the default), diff, extract and browse. Merge takes a file and a patch, or three files, and produces a three-way merge with word-level comparison. Diff reports word-wise or line-wise differences in a unified-diff style. Extract pulls one branch out of a patch or merge file. Browse is an interactive mode for stepping through a set of patches, and its help text says it 'will eventually allow limited editing'.

The idea underneath is that a diff does not have to be a list of lines. Change the unit of comparison from lines to words and a whole class of conflicts shrinks or disappears. The source tree has files named bestmatch.c, merge2.c and patch_depends.c, which hint at how the matching works, but the README does not explain the algorithm, so reading the source is the way in.

entry.whats_unique: Most patch tools match whole lines. Wiggle matches words, so it can apply a hunk whose context has changed slightly and still produce a three-way merge with word-level conflict markers.
entry.caveats: Maintained slowly and niche; browse mode editing is unfinished, and the README is mostly help text rather than an explanation of how it works.
